clue.text: Subject of a striking offer

parts.note: the Sermon on the Mount tells the struck to offer the second side of the face to the striker

explanation.surface: Someone is the topic of a remarkable proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' reads as 'remarkable', but here it means hitting: the offer is to be hit again, on the other side of the face.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gospel advice is to turn this to an attacker, offering it for a second blow.

clue.text: It runs through one's mind

parts.note: pictures a railway service running through the head, but describes a sequence of connected ideas

explanation.surface: Something keeps passing through a person's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' suggests a locomotive on rails; the phrase for a linked sequence of ideas uses the railway image.
explanation.definitionFit: A connected sequence of ideas is pictured as carriages following an engine through the head.

clue.text: Jostle from below

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the next word, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is shoved by a person underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells you to make the answer out of the letters of BELOW.
explanation.definitionFit: To push others aside with the arm's joint is to shove or jostle through a crowd.

clue.text: Perjurer sounds as intoxicated as grain can make him

indicators.note: the clue tells us the name is spoken like the phrase that follows

parts.words: as intoxicated as grain can make him
parts.note: drunk as oats might make him: 'tight as oats', tight meaning drunk

explanation.surface: A liar under oath seems as drunk as cereal could make a man.
explanation.walkthrough: TITUS OATES, who invented the Popish Plot of 1678, is the most famous perjurer in English history; 'tight as oats' sounds like his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventeenth-century fabricator of the Popish Plot swore false evidence that sent innocent men to execution.

clue.text: Alfred Jingle and Rachael Wardle were

definitions.text: Alfred Jingle and Rachael Wardle were

parts.words: Alfred Jingle and Rachael Wardle were
parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers the rogue Jingle runs off secretly with the spinster Rachael Wardle

explanation.surface: Two Dickens characters were something together.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pickwick Papers, Jingle persuades Rachael Wardle to run away with him to be married, hoping for her money.
explanation.definitionFit: Couples who run off secretly to marry are runaways of this kind, as the two Pickwick characters were.

clue.text: The kind of vote a founder member might give ?

definitions.text: The kind of vote a founder member might give ?

parts.words: The kind of vote a founder member might give
parts.note: a chairman's deciding vote, and also what a metal-founder produces from a mould

explanation.surface: An original member of a society settles a tied ballot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Founder member' suggests an original member of a club, but a founder also pours molten metal into moulds; the chair's deciding vote shares its name with his product.
explanation.definitionFit: A deciding ballot given by the chair is so called, and a metal object poured in a mould is one too.

clue.text: Pat takes her on his knee

definitions.text: Pat takes her on his knee

parts.words: Pat takes her on his knee
parts.note: a girl's name placed after PAT spells the medical term for the kneecap

explanation.surface: An Irishman sits a girl on his lap.
explanation.walkthrough: Put PAT before the girl's name and you get the kneecap's Latin name: Pat 'takes her on' and makes part of his knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, here supplied as the ending of the bone at the front of the knee.

clue.text: Range of the cook's activities

parts.note: suggests the scope of what a cook does, but means the iron stove itself

explanation.surface: Everything a cook does, from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' reads as 'scope', but means a cooking stove; a kitchener is an old name for a kitchen range.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitchener was a closed cast-iron cooking stove, the range on which a cook worked.

clue.text: Armour of the mailed fist ?

parts.note: suggests medieval chain mail on the hand, but means metal rings worn over the fingers to punch

explanation.surface: A knight's protection for an armoured hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mailed fist' calls up knightly gauntlets; the answer is the metal grip a street fighter slips over the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal bands worn over the fingers protect and harden a punching hand, like armour on a fist.

clue.text: Caesar, according to Brutus

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Brutus justifies the murder by saying Caesar sought too much power

explanation.surface: How one Roman described another.
explanation.walkthrough: Brutus tells the Roman crowd, 'as he was ambitious, I slew him'; Mark Antony then mocks the claim.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutus's charge against Caesar was an eagerness for power and a crown.

clue.text: The language of a dog ?

parts.note: suggests barking, but refers to the phrase for bad, made-up Roman speech

explanation.surface: What tongue does a dog speak?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog Latin' is mock or badly-made Latin; the clue reads the phrase as the speech of a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude imitation of the Roman tongue is called dog Latin, so a dog's language is that tongue.

clue.text: "____ and blind-worms, do no wrong." (M.N. Dream)

definitions.text: "____ and blind-worms, do no wrong." (M.N. Dream)

parts.words: "____ and blind-worms, do no wrong." (M.N. Dream)
parts.note: a fairy lullaby in A Midsummer Night's Dream warns small creatures away from the sleeping Titania

explanation.surface: Complete a line from Shakespeare's fairy play.
explanation.walkthrough: The fairies sing 'Spotted snakes with double tongue... Newts and blind-worms, do no wrong, Come not near our fairy queen.'
explanation.definitionFit: Small amphibians, efts, named alongside slow-worms in the fairies' lullaby to Titania.

clue.text: Even the most gullible shouldn't be taken in by it

definitions.text: Even the most gullible shouldn't be taken in by it

parts.words: Even the most gullible shouldn't be taken in by it
parts.note: 'taken in' suggests being fooled, but literally means led inward, which a way out cannot do

explanation.surface: A trick so obvious nobody could fall for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' reads as 'deceived'; literally a way out leads nobody in, however gullible.
explanation.definitionFit: A way out of a building leads people outside, never inside.

clue.text: Smart bit of psychical research

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is taken, a run of their letters

explanation.surface: A clever fragment of parapsychology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit of' points to letters inside 'psychical'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stylish and elegant, as in smartly dressed.

clue.text: This science, however complicated, is still A.B.C. to the gunner

indicators.note: the letters that follow are to be jumbled up, however tangled the result

parts.note: the three letters themselves

explanation.surface: However hard the science looks, a gunner finds it as easy as the alphabet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'however complicated' tells you to rearrange IS STILL ABC; 'to the gunner' completes the picture of the science of projectiles.
explanation.definitionFit: The science of projectiles in flight, which a gunner must master.

clue.text: Masonry's highest decorations ?

parts.note: suggests the top honours of Freemasonry, but means carved ornaments on top of stonework

explanation.surface: The top awards a Freemason can earn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Masonry' suggests the Freemasons and their honours; the answer is the ornament crowning a spire or gable.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornaments carved at the very top of a pinnacle, gable or spire.

clue.text: People of the same calling

parts.note: suggests colleagues in one profession, but means people called by the same name

explanation.surface: Workers who share a trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calling' reads as 'profession'; here it means what someone is called.
explanation.definitionFit: People who share a name with another person are called by the same word.

clue.text: It used to keep one in touch with the enemy at sea

definitions.text: It used to keep one in touch with the enemy at sea

parts.words: It used to keep one in touch with the enemy at sea
parts.note: suggests a means of signalling, but describes a hooked iron thrown to hold an enemy ship alongside

explanation.surface: An old way of staying in contact with a foe in naval warfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In touch' sounds like communication; old warships threw a hooked iron to hold an enemy vessel alongside for boarding.
explanation.definitionFit: A small multi-pronged anchor or grappling iron, thrown to hook and hold another vessel.

clue.text: Emphatically he might be Flemish

indicators.note: the letters of the next word could become the answer if rearranged

explanation.surface: A man could, stressed, turn out to be from Flanders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might be' asks you to rearrange FLEMISH.
explanation.definitionFit: The emphatic form of the masculine pronoun, as in 'he did it all by his own hand'.

clue.text: By an arresting blonde ?

parts.note: pictures a striking light-haired woman, but means a fair-haired policeman making an arrest

explanation.surface: Caught by a striking fair-haired woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arresting' reads as 'striking'; a fair (blonde) cop arrests you, and 'it's a fair cop' is what a caught criminal says.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang admission of a justified arrest; read literally, a light-haired policeman.

clue.text: She's right in the middle oddly enough

indicators.note: strange behaviour signals that the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A woman sits right in the centre, strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' tells you to rearrange R and MIDDLE together.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, standing for a female person.

clue.text: A gleeman might render such a medley

indicators.note: to render is to translate or alter, so the word's letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A minstrel might sing a mixed collection of songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might render' asks you to rearrange GLEEMAN, an old word for a minstrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixture of varied things, a jumble; borrowed from French.

clue.text: Bear aloft

parts.note: suggests lifting something up, but means the bear found in the night sky

explanation.surface: Hold something up high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' reads as a verb, 'carry'; it is the animal, as a constellation in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin name for the bear, given to the Great and Little Bear constellations overhead.

clue.text: Have a breather, and a drink at the same time

definitions.meaning: an organ a fish breathes through
a small measure of spirits, a quarter of a pint

explanation.surface: Pause for breath and have a quick drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have a breather' suggests a rest, but a breather here is a fish's breathing organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish breathes through these organs, and a quarter-pint measure of liquor is called by the same word.

clue.text: Philosophers for a season ?

definitions.meaning: used for seasoning food, as a herb

explanation.surface: Thinkers who are only in fashion for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for a season' suggests a limited time, but means for seasoning food: the herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Wise thinkers are so called, and a grey-green herb used to season food bears the same name.

clue.text: Shining example to the kids ?

parts.note: suggests a role model for children, but means a polished finish on goatskin leather

explanation.surface: Someone who sets a fine example to the young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' reads as 'children', but kid is goatskin leather; glacé kid is the glossy kind.
explanation.definitionFit: French for iced or glazed, used of leather or fruit given a smooth shiny surface.

clue.text: Something of growing concern to the family

definitions.text: Something of growing concern to the family

parts.words: Something of growing concern to the family
parts.note: suggests a worry for the household, but means the branching chart of ancestry, which keeps growing

explanation.surface: A worry that keeps getting bigger for a household.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growing concern' reads as 'increasing worry'; it is the family tree, which grows and concerns the family.
explanation.definitionFit: A family's genealogy is drawn as branches from a trunk, a woody plant.

clue.text: One might be encountered in any walk of life

definitions.text: One might be encountered in any walk of life

parts.words: One might be encountered in any walk of life
parts.note: the idiom means any profession or class, but read literally it is a rambler met on any walk

explanation.surface: You can meet this sort of person anywhere in society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk of life' means occupation or class; taken literally, it is anyone out walking.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler or walker, the person you meet on a country walk.

clue.text: He's not angry when he gets cross

definitions.text: He's not angry when he gets cross

parts.words: He's not angry when he gets cross
parts.note: 'cross' reads as angry, but means a voter's mark on a ballot beside a name

explanation.surface: A calm man who stays good-tempered when annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets cross' reads as 'becomes angry'; a person standing for election is glad to get a voter's X.
explanation.definitionFit: A person standing for election hopes voters will mark crosses beside his name.

clue.text: Macbeth was vociferously condemned to it

definitions.text: Macbeth was vociferously condemned to it

parts.words: Macbeth was vociferously condemned to it
parts.note: after the murder of Duncan, Macbeth hears a voice cry 'Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep'

explanation.surface: A loud sentence passed on a Scottish king.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth reports hearing a voice cry 'Sleep no more' to all the house: he is loudly condemned to be unable to rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Insomnia, the state of being unable to rest at night, which the voice decreed for Macbeth.
